items.prompt: What do the creatures clustered around a deep-sea hydrothermal vent live on?

options.label: Sugar drifting down from sunlit water far above
options.feedback: Almost nothing from the surface survives the fall to that depth; the vent community feeds on something made on the spot.

options.label: Bacteria that build food from the vent's chemicals
options.feedback: Those bacteria turn the vent's dissolved minerals into sugar, and everything around the vent eats them or their host.

options.label: Heat radiating from the vent itself
options.feedback: Heat can warm a body, but no animal digests heat directly; it still needs a meal built of matter.

options.label: Minerals absorbed straight through their skin
options.feedback: Minerals alone are not food; an animal's cells need sugar to burn, and no skin absorbs that ready-made from vent water.

items.ok_line: A whole community feeding on bacteria that never saw the sun.
items.ko_line: Something at the very bottom of that food web has to build sugar out of raw chemicals, since no light reaches that deep.
items.exp_title: A food web with no sunlight at its base
items.exp_text: Hydrothermal vents pour out water rich in dissolved chemicals such as hydrogen sulphide, and dense mats of bacteria coat the rock around them. Those bacteria convert the chemicals into sugar, and the tube worms, clams and crabs of the vent either filter the bacteria from the water, host them inside their own bodies, or eat the animals that do. What the vent community lives on is bacteria that build food from the vent's chemicals.

items.prompt: How do vent bacteria build sugar without any light?

options.label: By absorbing sugar dissolved in the vent water
options.feedback: Vent water carries minerals and gases, not ready-made sugar; the bacteria have to build it themselves.

options.label: By breaking down the bodies of dead animals nearby
options.feedback: That is what a scavenger or decomposer does; vent bacteria build new sugar rather than recycling old bodies.

options.label: By fermenting the sulphur in the rock
options.feedback: Fermentation breaks down existing sugar for a quick payoff; it cannot build new sugar out of raw minerals.

options.label: By releasing energy from a chemical reaction with hydrogen sulphide
options.feedback: That released energy powers the same kind of carbon-joining that a plant's light-driven energy powers.

items.ok_line: Energy from a chemical reaction instead of energy from light.
items.ko_line: Somewhere a source of energy has to power the joining of carbon atoms into sugar. Ask what supplies it here.
items.exp_text: A plant's leaf uses the energy of sunlight to join carbon atoms into sugar. A vent bacterium instead lets hydrogen sulphide react with oxygen dissolved in the seawater, and that reaction releases energy the same way burning fuel does. The bacterium spends that released energy to join carbon dioxide into sugar, building its food by releasing energy from a chemical reaction with hydrogen sulphide.

items.prompt: What is the main source of food for animals living on the ocean floor far from any vent?

options.label: Debris and dead plankton drifting down from the surface
options.feedback: Dead organisms and waste sinking from the sunlit layers above supply almost everything the deep floor eats.

options.label: Sugar made by bacteria living in the mud
options.feedback: Ordinary sea-floor mud lacks the chemical fuel that vent bacteria run on, so this route barely feeds the wider deep floor.

options.label: Minerals dissolved in the cold water
options.feedback: Dissolved minerals are not food; an animal still needs matter its cells can burn for energy.

options.label: Algae growing on the sea floor itself
options.feedback: Algae need light to grow, and none reaches the deep floor, so none grows there.

items.ok_line: A slow, steady rain from the sunlit world above.
items.ko_line: Away from a vent's chemical fuel, the deep floor has to be fed by something falling from above.
items.exp_title: Snow that falls from life, not weather
items.exp_text: In the sunlit layers near the surface, tiny drifting organisms live, die and produce waste in vast numbers. Their remains sink slowly through the water column over days or weeks, drifting down as a constant shower of pale flecks that scientists call marine snow. Far from any vent, the ocean floor's animals live mainly on this debris and dead plankton drifting down from the surface.

items.prompt: Why are so many cave-dwelling animals pale and lacking in colour?

options.label: Cold cave air stops pigment from forming
options.feedback: Cave temperature has no chemical effect on pigment; plenty of animals in cold, lit places stay richly coloured.

options.label: Pigment serves no purpose in permanent darkness and stops being built
options.feedback: With nothing to see it and no light to filter, pigment costs the animal resources for no benefit, and over generations it is lost.

options.label: The rock in caves bleaches their skin over time
options.feedback: Rock has no bleaching action on living tissue; an animal's colour is set by what pigment its own cells build.

options.label: They shed their colour each time they moult
options.feedback: Moulting animals outside caves regrow their normal colour every time; the loss in caves is not tied to moulting at all.

items.ok_line: A feature that costs something and does nothing, quietly dropped.
items.ko_line: Think about what pigment is even for, and whether that job still exists where no light ever reaches.
items.exp_title: A cost with no benefit, gradually dropped
items.exp_text: Pigment such as melanin normally serves to absorb light, whether to shield cells from it or to display a colour that other animals can see. In permanent darkness neither job is possible, so building pigment costs an animal resources while returning nothing. Generation after generation, cave lineages lose it, which is why so many cave-dwelling animals end up pale and lacking in colour.

items.prompt: Why do many cave-dwelling animals have small, non-functional eyes or none at all?

options.label: Building and maintaining eyes costs the body resources that darkness makes worthless
options.feedback: An eye needs constant upkeep to work, and where there is nothing to see, that cost stops paying for itself.

options.label: The rock walls of caves damage eyes on contact
options.feedback: Cave animals move carefully using other senses; eye loss shows up even in species that rarely touch a wall at all.

options.label: Cave air lacks the oxygen that eyes need
options.feedback: Cave air holds enough oxygen for every other organ; eyes are not singled out by any shortage of it.

options.label: Their ancestors were never able to see in the first place
options.feedback: Many cave species descend from sighted surface ancestors with working eyes, which is clear from the eye remnants some still carry.

items.ok_line: An organ upkeep cannot justify once there is nothing to see.
items.ko_line: An eye is not a one-time feature; it takes continuous energy to run, in a place with nothing to look at.
items.exp_title: An organ that stops earning its keep
items.exp_text: A working eye is expensive to grow and to run, since the nerve tissue behind it demands a steady supply of energy. In total darkness that expense buys nothing, because there is no light for it to detect. Across generations, animals that spent less on eyes and more elsewhere left more offspring, so cave lineages end up with small, non-functional eyes or none at all because building and maintaining them costs resources that darkness makes worthless.

items.prompt: How do many blind cave animals find food and avoid obstacles without sight?

options.label: By memorising the exact layout of the cave
options.feedback: Caves shift with falling debris and flowing water, and many cave animals also range into passages they have never entered.

options.label: By following scent trails left by other cave animals only
options.feedback: Scent trails help track other animals specifically, but they say nothing about a wall ahead or the shape of the passage.

options.label: By sensing vibrations, currents, and touch through long feelers or sensitive skin
options.feedback: Extended antennae, whiskers or skin studded with sensory cells pick up ripples and touch that sight would otherwise have handled.

options.label: By echolocation, the same way bats hunt in open air
options.feedback: Most cave animals lack any sound-based ranging system; that method is limited to a small number of specialised cave bats.

items.ok_line: Touch and vibration take over the job sight would have done.
items.ko_line: Sight is gone, but the surrounding water or air still carries information, if something on the animal's body can feel it.
items.exp_text: Blind cave animals commonly carry long antennae, whiskers, or skin covered in sensory cells that respond to the faintest touch, current, or vibration. A cave fish, for instance, senses changes in water pressure along its flanks well before it would ever bump into a wall or another fish. Without sight, they find food and avoid obstacles by sensing vibrations, currents, and touch through long feelers or sensitive skin.

items.prompt: Why is the deep open ocean completely dark below a certain depth?

options.label: Because plankton near the surface consume all incoming light
options.feedback: Plankton absorb some light for their own use, but they are far too few and thin a layer to account for total darkness below.

options.label: Because water absorbs and scatters sunlight as it travels down
options.feedback: Every metre of water removes a portion of the remaining light, so within a few hundred metres almost none is left.

options.label: Because the ocean floor blocks light from reflecting back up
options.feedback: The floor lies far beneath the point where light disappears; reflection from it plays no part in how dark the water above becomes.

options.label: Because the sun's rays cannot penetrate salt water at all
options.feedback: Salt water lets light through readily near the surface, as any sunlit shallow sea shows; it is depth, not salt, that empties the light out.

items.ok_line: Light disappears gradually, metre by metre, before it ever reaches the floor.
items.ko_line: Nothing needs to consume or block the light on purpose. Ask what water itself does to light passing through it.
items.exp_title: Light used up on the way down
items.exp_text: Water is not perfectly clear: every metre a beam of sunlight travels through, some of it is absorbed and some is scattered off in other directions. Red light is lost within the first few tens of metres, and even the blue-green light that penetrates furthest fades until, by around a thousand metres, essentially none is left. The deep ocean is dark because water absorbs and scatters sunlight as it travels down.

items.prompt: Why do most animals living in the deep, sunless open ocean lack any colour pattern for camouflage?

options.label: A colour pattern would require sunlight to be visible at all
options.feedback: Without light to reflect off it, a pattern of stripes or spots looks identical to plain skin, so camouflage of that kind has nothing to work with.

options.label: Cold water dissolves any pigment they carry
options.feedback: Cold does not dissolve pigment; plenty of cold-water surface animals near the sunlit zone stay boldly patterned.

options.label: Predators there hunt by scent, not sight
options.feedback: Some deep predators do rely on scent, but many others hunt visually, using bioluminescent light rather than sunlight.

options.label: Their prey cannot see colour either
options.feedback: What prey can or cannot see affects whether colour helps them hide, but it does not explain why the predator's own pattern would be pointless too.

items.ok_line: A pattern that needs light to be seen is no use where there is none.
items.ko_line: Camouflage works by matching what light reveals. Ask what happens to that trick once there is no sunlight left to reveal anything.
items.exp_title: A disguise with nothing to catch
items.exp_text: Camouflage in a sunlit habitat works because a pattern of light and dark blends an animal into light and dark surroundings, deceiving an eye that is reading reflected sunlight. In the deep ocean there is no sunlight left to reflect, so a striped or spotted pattern would look no different from a plain one. Most deep-ocean animals lack a colour pattern because one would require sunlight to be visible at all.

items.prompt: Why do tube worms living at hydrothermal vents have no mouth or gut?

options.label: They absorb all their nutrients directly through their skin
options.feedback: Their skin plays no digestive role; the worm's food is processed inside a dedicated internal organ, not absorbed across its surface.

options.label: They survive on stored fat from their larval stage alone
options.feedback: A store of fat from the larval stage would be used up long before an adult tube worm's years-long life at the vent are over.

options.label: They host food-making bacteria inside their own body instead of eating
options.feedback: Packed into a special internal organ, those bacteria build sugar from vent chemicals and pass it straight to the worm's cells.

options.label: They draw energy from the heat of the vent water
options.feedback: Heat can warm a body but cannot be digested into the sugar an animal's cells need to run on.

items.ok_line: A worm that grows its own bacterial pantry instead of a gut.
items.ko_line: A tube worm has no mouth, so whatever feeds it must already be living inside its own body.
items.exp_title: A body built around its bacteria
items.exp_text: A tube worm's larva has a working mouth and gut, but once it settles near a vent it takes in vent bacteria and grows a special internal organ, called a trophosome, to hold them. Packed inside that organ, the bacteria build sugar from the vent's dissolved chemicals and pass much of it directly into the worm's tissues. The adult worm needs no mouth or gut because it hosts food-making bacteria inside its own body instead of eating.

items.prompt: Why can life at a hydrothermal vent thrive without ever depending on the sun?

options.label: Vent water is warm enough to replace the sun's energy entirely
options.feedback: Warmth alone cannot power the building of sugar; a cell still needs a chemical reaction it can extract usable energy from.

options.label: Vent bacteria draw energy from chemical reactions in the vent water itself
options.feedback: That released chemical energy powers the same carbon-joining that light powers in a leaf, making sunlight unnecessary at the base of this food web.

options.label: Vent animals eat the minerals that erupt from the vent directly
options.feedback: Minerals are not food an animal can digest; something still has to convert them into sugar first, and that step is done by bacteria, not by the animals themselves.

options.label: Vent communities are fed entirely by debris sinking from the surface
options.feedback: That sinking debris feeds the wider ocean floor, but a hydrothermal vent's own bacterial food web works independently of it.

items.ok_line: An energy source built into the water itself, with no sunlight required.
items.ko_line: The base of this food web still has to be something that converts raw chemicals into sugar, using energy from somewhere other than light.
items.exp_title: An independent base to the food web
items.exp_text: Every other food web on Earth traces back to something using light to build sugar, but a vent's bacteria instead react hydrogen sulphide from the vent water with dissolved oxygen and capture the energy that reaction releases. That captured energy powers the joining of carbon dioxide into sugar, exactly as light's energy does inside a leaf. Vent life needs no sun because its bacteria draw energy from chemical reactions in the vent water itself.
